items.title: Lesson 2, "Applying Practices: Modeling Fission, Fusion, and Radioactive Decay" and "Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question": A team is deciding whether a proposed fission reactor design could work. What information from this lesson helps answer the unit and module questions, and what should a model of one fission show?

body.html: Nuclear reactions conserve nucleon number and charge, and the mass lost becomes energy.

Useful information: fission of uranium-235 releases about 180 MeV per nucleus; each fission releases two or three neutrons that can cause more fissions (a chain reaction); a moderator slows the neutrons and control rods absorb them. A model of one fission should show a neutron entering a large nucleus, the nucleus splitting into two middle-sized nuclei plus free neutrons, and the energy released, with nucleon number and charge balanced before and after.

answer.html: The lesson shows that a reactor gets energy from the mass lost in fission (about 180 MeV per uranium-235 nucleus), that the chain reaction is sustained by released neutrons, and that moderators and control rods let operators control it. A good model shows the particle counts before and after and the energy released.

check.html: Each fact is stated in the lesson.

items.title: Lesson 2, "Get It?" (page 681): List four ways the nucleus of an atom can change, and state how 𝑍 and 𝐴 change in each.

answer.html: (1) Alpha emission: 𝑍 decreases by 2 and 𝐴 by 4. (2) Beta-minus decay (a neutron becomes a proton): 𝑍 increases by 1, 𝐴 unchanged. (3) Positron emission (a proton becomes a neutron): 𝑍 decreases by 1, 𝐴 unchanged. (4) Gamma emission: energy only, so 𝑍 and 𝐴 are unchanged. A nucleus can also change by absorbing a particle, by splitting (fission), or by combining with another nucleus (fusion).

check.html: Each is described in this lesson.

items.title: Lesson 2, "Get It?" (page 684): Sample X has a half-life of 6.0 hours and sample Y has a half-life of 6.0 days. Both start with the same number of radioactive nuclei. Compare their half-lives and their initial activities, and tell which has the greater activity after 12 hours has passed.

body.html: 𝑇<sub>𝑋</sub>= 6.0 h; 𝑇<sub>𝑌</sub>= 6.0 days = 144 h; equal numbers of nuclei at the start.
Half-life is a time; activity is a rate (decays per second, in becquerels) proportional to the number of radioactive nuclei present and inversely proportional to the half-life.
For equal numbers of nuclei, the activity ratio is

After 12 h, X has gone through 2 half-lives, so its activity is <sup>1</sup> <sub>4</sub> of its start. Y has gone through only 12 / 144 = 0.083 half-lives, so (<sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>)<sup>0.083</sup> = 0.94 of its start remains. Then 𝐴<sub>𝑋</sub>/ 𝐴<sub>𝑌</sub>= 24 × 0.25 / 0.94 = 6.4.

answer.html: Alike: both describe how fast nuclei decay, and each activity halves after one half-life. Different: half-life is a fixed time for the isotope, while activity is a rate that depends on how much is present and falls with time. X starts with 24 times the activity of Y, and after 12 hours X still has about 6.4 times the activity of Y.

check.html: The short-lived sample is always the more active one for equal numbers of nuclei.

items.title: Lesson 2, "Get It?" (page 685): A patient has a thyroid tumor and another has a deep brain tumor. Summarize three ways radiation can be used to destroy cancer cells and say which fits each patient best.

answer.html: (1) Gamma rays from cobalt-60 are aimed at the tumor from outside the body, which suits a deep brain tumor when beams from several directions are focused on it. (2) Radioactive iodine is swallowed or injected and accumulates in the thyroid, destroying thyroid cancer cells, so it suits the thyroid patient. (3) A particle accelerator produces a beam of particles that deposit their energy in the cancerous tissue, which can also be aimed at a deep tumor. Cancer cells are more sensitive because they divide more often.

check.html: All three are methods listed in the lesson; iodine goes to the thyroid because the thyroid takes up iodine.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 12 "Infer": Operators of a reactor see the power level rising slowly. Which way should they move the neutron-absorbing control rods, and why might the rods also be fully inserted in an emergency?

answer.html: They should insert the rods farther into the core. The rods absorb neutrons, so fewer neutrons are left to cause new fissions and the chain reaction slows. Fully inserting them absorbs so many neutrons that the chain reaction stops, which shuts the reactor down.

check.html: Each fission releases two or three neutrons; if more than one of them goes on to cause a fission, power grows, so removing neutrons reduces it.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) 33: Why doesn't a tank of deuterium gas at room temperature (300 K) undergo fusion, even though deuterium is used as fusion fuel? Compare the average thermal energy per particle, 3

body.html: Fusion requires the nuclei to get close enough for the strong force to act, which means overcoming their electric repulsion. That takes very high thermal energy.

answer.html: At 300 K the nuclei have only about 0.04 eV of thermal energy, nowhere near enough to approach each other against their electric repulsion, so no fusion occurs. items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) 35: A beta emitter (a strontium-90 source) is mounted on one plate of a capacitor, and the 𝛽− particles strike the other plate. As a result, there is a potential difference between the plates. Explain and predict which plate has the more positive potential.

body.html: A beta-minus particle is an electron (charge −𝑒). Charge moves from the emitter plate to the other plate with the electrons.
The emitter plate loses negative charge, so it becomes positive; the plate struck by the electrons gains negative charge, so it becomes negative.

answer.html: The emitter plate is at the more positive potential, and the plate that receives the electrons is more negative.

check.html: This is the opposite of an alpha emitter, whose particles carry positive charge to the far plate.

items.title: Lesson 2, "Get It?" (page 684): Compare and contrast half-life and activity

body.html: Half-life is a time; activity is a rate (decays per second, in becquerels). Activity is proportional to the number of radioactive nuclei present.

Both are tied to how fast nuclei decay: a short half-life means high activity for a given amount. But half-life is a fixed property of the isotope, while activity falls by half every half-life as the sample shrinks.

answer.html: Alike: both describe the rate of decay, and the activity halves after each half-life. Different: half-life is the (constant) time for half the nuclei to decay and is measured in time units; activity is the number of decays per second (Bq), depends on how much of the isotope is present, and decreases with time.

check.html: Units differ (s versus decays/s).

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) 29: How can an electron come out of a nucleus without being inside it?

body.html: The electron is created at the moment of decay, not stored in the nucleus.

In 𝛽<sup>−</sup> decay a neutron changes into a proton; to conserve charge, an electron (and an antineutrino) is produced and emitted. In quark language, a down quark becomes an up quark and a W<sup>−</sup> boson, which decays into the electron and antineutrino.

answer.html: The electron is created in the decay of a neutron into a proton, with an antineutrino; charge is conserved because 0 →+ 1 + ( −1). It was not in the nucleus before.

check.html: The nucleus after the decay has one more proton.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) 30: Alpha decay of polonium-210

body.html: Po has 𝑍= 84. Alpha emission gives 𝐴= 206, 𝑍= 82 (lead).

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) 31: Time for iodine-131 to fall to three-eighths of its activity

body.html: 𝑇<sub>1 / 2</sub> = 8.07 days. Fraction remaining = 3 / 8 = 0.375. From Figure 9, 0.375 lies between 1 / 2 (1 half-life) and 1 / 4 (2 half-lives), at about 1.4 half-lives.

check.html: Between 8.07 days (one half-life) and 16.1 days (two half-lives).

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) 32: Why not lead as a moderator?

body.html: A moderator slows neutrons by collisions. A neutron transfers the most energy when it collides with a nucleus of nearly its own mass (light atoms).
A neutron bouncing off a very heavy lead nucleus (mass about 200 u) loses almost no speed, like a ball bouncing off a wall.

answer.html: Lead nuclei are far more massive than neutrons, so neutrons bounce off with almost no loss of energy and are not slowed. A moderator needs light atoms such as hydrogen in water.

check.html: Compare with the book's use of water as moderator.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) 33: Why doesn't helium in a balloon fuse?

answer.html: Fusion needs the nuclei to get close enough that the strong force acts, which means overcoming their electric repulsion; this requires temperatures of millions of kelvin. Helium in a balloon is near room temperature, so its nuclei have far too little energy to come close.

check.html: Compare 300 K with about 2 × 10<sup>7</sup> K in the Sun's core.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) 34: Energy of the first fusion reaction in the Sun

body.html: Atomic masses: 𝑚(H-1) = 1.007825 u, 𝑚(H-2) = 2.014102 u; electron mass 𝑚<sub>e</sub> = 9.109 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>31</sup> kg = 0.000549 u. The neutrino mass is negligible.

Energy released = (mass before − mass after)𝑐<sup>2</sup>. Using atomic masses, the two hydrogen atoms bring two electrons, but the deuterium atom keeps only one, so the leftover electron mass plus the positron's mass (two electron masses in all) must be subtracted from the atomic-mass difference.

check.html: Small compared with the 25 MeV for the full chain; this step is the slow one and not very energetic.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) 35: Alpha emitters in smoke detectors

body.html: An alpha particle is positively charged (+2𝑒). Charge moves from the emitter plate to the other plate with the alpha particles.
The emitter plate loses positive charge (it becomes negative) and the plate struck by the alphas gains positive charge.

answer.html: The plate that receives the alpha particles (opposite the emitter) is at the more positive potential; the emitter plate is more negative.

check.html: When smoke absorbs the alphas the current changes, which triggers the alarm.
